title: Elevated blood lead levels among pregnant women in Amran, Yemen: Socio-demographic correlates and associations with a history of spontaneous abortion
content:
by Lina Qasem, Abdulsalam Al-Shami, Tawfeek A. A. Yahya, Lutfi AS. Al-Maktari, Mohammed Al-Maqhafi, Akram Al-Marqasi

Background

Lead exposure in pregnant women is a critical public health concern, particularly in resource-limited settings where environmental regulations are less stringent. Prenatal lead exposure (Pb) is associated with various adverse maternal and fetal outcomes. Therefore, this study aimed to assess blood lead levels (BLLs) among pregnant women in Amran, Yemen, and to identify health risks associated with environmental, behavioral, and socio-demographic factors.

Methods

A cross-sectional multi-center study was conducted between August and November 2024, involving a sample of 150 pregnant women (aged 20–41 years) recruited across public and private healthcare facilities in Amran. Data were collected via structured questionnaires, and venous blood samples collected in K2 EDTA were analyzed using atomic absorption spectrophotometry (UNICAM 929AA). Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS version 24, with a significance threshold of P < 0.05.

Results

The results revealed a critically high prevalence of heavy metal exposure, with 82.7% of the sampled cohort exhibiting BLLs above 10 µg/dL. The median BLL of the sample was 40.8 µg/dL (IQR: 19.0–62.0), ranging from 1.0 to 143.0 µg/dL. Multivariable logistic regression identified a history of spontaneous abortion as a significant independent factor strongly associated with elevated BLLs (AOR = 5.88, 95% CI: 1.66–20.89, p = 0.006). Notably, the wide confidence interval indicates statistical imprecision due to limited reference cell counts. Elevated blood lead levels were positively, but non-significantly, associated with residential proximity to petrol stations and battery recycling sites, para-occupational exposure, and current smoking. Conversely, maternal age, formal education level, and housing type showed no significant independent association with lead levels.

Conclusion

This study identifies a severe public health crisis in Amran, highlighting the need for immediate investigations to identify sources of lead exposure, strengthened environmental regulation, and the integration of routine blood lead level screening into antenatal care. Such measures could help identify women with critically elevated BLLs who require close monitoring and follow-up.
author: Lina Qasem
